paragraphs.title: A Heart Ready for Song and a Plea for God's Revelation

easy.explanation: He says, “O God, my heart is fixed.”
easy.q: What does the psalmist say is fixed?

easy.explanation: The psalmist says, “Awake, psaltery and harp.”
He will praise the LORD “among the people” and “among the nations.”
easy.q: Among whom will the psalmist praise the LORD?

medium.explanation: His fixed heart leads him to sing and give praise.
medium.q: What does the fixed heart prepare the psalmist to do?

medium.explanation: He declares that God’s mercy is great and His truth reaches unto the clouds.
medium.q: What does the psalmist praise about God?

answers: A request for God to hide
A request for God to descend
A plea for God’s glory to be lifted above all
medium.explanation: The psalmist asks God to be exalted above the heavens and for His glory to be above all the earth.
medium.q: What does the request “Be thou exalted” express?

answers: It moves from personal readiness to public praise
It moves from battle to dividing the land
It moves from fear to describing enemies
challenge.explanation: The psalmist begins with his fixed heart and then promises praise among the people and nations.
challenge.q: How does the passage move from the psalmist’s heart to the nations?

answers: They show that God is both gracious and faithful
They identify the tribes of Israel
challenge.explanation: The passage joins God’s great mercy with His abiding truth.
challenge.q: What is the significance of mentioning both mercy and truth?

answers: To deliver God’s beloved and answer him
challenge.explanation: The request follows the words, “That thy beloved may be delivered.”
challenge.q: Why does the psalmist ask God to save with His right hand?

paragraphs.title: The Promise of Victory and the Division of the Land

answers: God has spoken in His holiness
easy.explanation: He says, “God hath spoken in his holiness; I will rejoice.”
easy.q: What causes the psalmist to rejoice?

answers: Shechem and the valley of Succoth
easy.explanation: The psalmist says, “I will divide Shechem, and mete out the valley of Succoth.”
easy.q: Which places are mentioned as being divided or measured?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “Ephraim also is the strength of mine head.”
easy.q: Which tribe is called the strength of the psalmist’s head?

answers: God’s word gives him reason to rejoice
medium.explanation: The psalmist rejoices because God has spoken in His holiness.
medium.q: What is the relationship between God’s spoken word and the psalmist’s rejoicing?

medium.explanation: To mete out is to measure or allot.
medium.q: What does “mete out” mean in this passage?

answers: As sources of strength and authority
medium.explanation: Gilead, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Judah are described in terms of possession, strength, and authority.
medium.q: How are the tribes in the passage presented?

answers: God’s word, division of the land, the tribes, and the enemies
The enemies, a prayer, and then God’s word
Song, instruments, and then a plea for salvation
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from God’s word to the land, the tribes, and the surrounding enemies.
challenge.q: What order of ideas appears in these verses?

answers: Judah is associated with rule and authority
challenge.explanation: A lawgiver is one who establishes or administers law, suggesting authority.
challenge.q: What does “Judah is my lawgiver” suggest?

challenge.explanation: The psalmist describes putting his shoe over Edom and triumphing over Philistia.
challenge.q: What attitude toward the enemies is expressed?

answers: Who will bring him into the strong city
easy.explanation: He asks, “Who will bring me into the strong city?”
easy.q: What does the psalmist ask first?

easy.explanation: He asks, “who will lead me into Edom?”
easy.q: Where does the psalmist ask to be led?

easy.explanation: The verse refers to “the strong city.”
easy.q: What kind of city is mentioned?

answers: To emphasize the need for leading and guidance
To explain the division of the land
medium.explanation: The psalmist asks both who will bring him and who will lead him.
medium.q: Why are two questions asked in succession?

medium.explanation: The phrase refers to being led into the strong city.
medium.q: What does “bring me into” mean in this context?

answers: They are two descriptions of mercy
They are destinations to which the psalmist seeks to be led
medium.explanation: The psalmist asks who will bring him into the city and lead him into Edom.
medium.q: How are the strong city and Edom related in the verse?

answers: The psalmist recognizes his need for a leader and guide
The psalmist is certain he needs no help
The psalmist wants to describe the dawn
challenge.explanation: The repeated question shows dependence on someone to lead and guide him.
challenge.q: What does the repeated question “Who” reveal?

answers: It continues the description of the instruments
It turns confidence about victory into a practical question about reaching the goal
It explains God’s mercy and truth
challenge.explanation: After speaking confidently about enemies, the psalmist asks who will lead him to the fortified place.
challenge.q: How does this verse relate to the previous description of victory?

answers: Reaching a strong city and entering Edom
challenge.explanation: The verse focuses on the challenge of reaching the strong city and Edom.
challenge.q: What central difficulty does the verse present?

easy.explanation: He asks whether God has cast them off and gone forth with their hosts.
easy.q: What does the psalmist say God had done?

easy.explanation: He says, “Give us help from trouble.”
easy.q: From what does the psalmist ask for help?

easy.explanation: The psalmist declares, “Through God we shall do valiantly.”
easy.q: What will they do through God?

answers: Rejection and trouble are contrasted with confidence in God
medium.explanation: The passage begins with the fear that God has cast them off and ends with confidence in God’s help.
medium.q: What contrast appears between the beginning and the end of the passage?

medium.explanation: To cast off is to reject or abandon.

answers: The request removes the need for courage
The request shows dependence on God, while the declaration shows confidence in the outcome
medium.explanation: The psalmist asks God for help and then declares that through God they will act valiantly.
medium.q: How are the request for help and the final declaration connected?

answers: Man is the only source of salvation
challenge.explanation: The statement contrasts the weakness of human help with dependence on God.
challenge.q: What does “vain is the help of man” teach about deliverance?

answers: He moves from asking for help to declaring confidence
He moves from joy to fear only
He moves from singing to dividing the land
challenge.explanation: He begins with the experience of rejection, asks for help, and ends confidently with God.
challenge.q: How does the psalmist’s attitude change in these verses?

challenge.explanation: The verse says, “for he it is that shall tread down our enemies.”
challenge.q: Who will tread down the enemies at the end?
